TechnologyTab.title: Some people's chats with Claude AI found publicly available online
TechnologyTab.text:
Hundreds of user conversations with Anthropic's popular artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot Claude were found to have been available to essentially anyone online.

Links to the chats, some of which included personal and work information, would show up if a user of a search engine like Google used a site-specific search term.

The searches showed Claude chats for which a user had decided to "share" a link had been saved by search engines like Google, leaving them accessible to the broader public.

The search availability of the chat logs was removed over the weekend, but many were saved and shared widely online.

A spokeswoman for Anthropic said that Claude users maintained control over if and when to share conversations they had with the chatbot.

She said links to conversations were "not guessable or discoverable unless people choose to share them themselves".

"When someone shares a conversation, they are making that content publicly accessible, and like other public web content, it may be archived by third-party services," the spokeswoman added.

The share option within Claude tells a user that "anyone with the link" may view the contents of that link, but does not explicitly state that the link may end up in Google and search results.

Users on Reddit initially discovered, external the publicly available chats, which covered more than 200 conversations with Claude across at least 25 pages of search results - some taking place just weeks ago.

In the conversations, users prompted the chatbot to respond to a wide array of topics.

Chat logs include a user asking Claude last year whether it wanted "to help me or do you want to help anthropic more?". The chatbot responded in part, saying "I experience something like wanting to help you".

In one conversation from April, a user prompted Claude to draft an unpublished blog post about cloud security involving details of a corporate project. In another from last month, a user asked Claude how to "become become Nine-tailed fox?", before clarifying they wanted to literally transform from human to the creature.

Claude first tried to show the user an AI-generated image claiming they had been given "fully functional fox powers!".

Other conversations with Claude included users seeking help with their CVs, including their names, contact information and work history. Some users even conducted what appeared to be proprietary research for their work, such as in healthcare, including transcripts of private conversations.

When OpenAI last year experienced an almost identical issue with ChatGPT chat logs being made publicly accessible, external, the company ultimately changed, external the ease with which such logs were accessible.

Grok, the AI chatbot within X, the social platform owned by Elon Musk, also last year saw hundreds of thousands of chat logs made publicly available though online search.

A spokesman for Google made clear to the BBC that the company does not control "what pages are made public on the web," saying instead that action comes from websites.

"We give site owners clear controls to decide whether pages can be crawled or indexed, and we always respect those directives."

As the search indexing of the chat logs is no longer occurring, it is likely Anthropic used available tools to quickly block the chat log links from search results. Google's process for a website owner to block a link, external is straightforward, but must be initiated by a website owner.

Other search engines like Bing, Brave and Duck Duck Go, through which the Claude chat logs also appeared, were approached for comment.

TechnologyTab.title: The great British switch-off: how floating retreats, mobile-free pubs and sauna book groups are liberating people from their phones
TechnologyTab.text:
There’s a ritual at the start of every event hosted by the Offline Project. Run by Pelé Zachariah, the activities vary – it could be a group walk, a collage‑making class or a supper club – but each one begins in the same way, *with an invitation to hand over your phone. Devices go in a lockbox. Once they’re all in, Zachariah closes the door and turns the key. “I don’t place them in for people, because it’s nice for them to physically put it in the box themselves, walk away, and think: for the next two or three hours, I’m fully present.”

He has been running these screen-free events in London since August 2025. First-timers can be apprehensive about being separated from their phone. “You can sense the vibe when they’re putting it away,” says Zachariah. “People have said to me, ‘I felt really weird’ or ‘I felt super uncomfortable for the first few minutes not having my phone on me.’ Then they’ll say, ‘I didn’t know how much I needed that.’”

Zachariah understands why people might find it difficult at first. “It’s very unnatural. You might put your phone in the living room while you work in the kitchen, but here you’re seeing it locked behind what is essentially a gate that you can’t access,” he says. But when people leave, they often say they would like to have their own phone lockbox, or tell him that they’re going to try to not look at their device until they get home. “It’s kind of sad that we have to literally lock our phones away. But people really crave that time.”

This is true for Jarred Laros, 31, who lives in Essex and has been a regular at the Offline Project since it launched. One of the first events he went to was a “paint and sip” evening, where an artist taught everyone how to paint a landscape scene with mountains, a river and a sunset. People sat around a table together, working on their canvases while having drinks and snacks, and getting to know each other. “I liked the idea of getting off my phone and being more intentional with how I’m spending my time. I would never try to teach myself how to paint, but doing that in a community setting is very easy-going. The conversation flows.”

Laros runs his own business, and spends a lot of time on his devices. “I’m always glued to a screen, whether it’s my iPad, my MacBook, my phone, or all three at the same time,” he says. “Outside of work, there’s the doomscroll that you succumb to. I go on Instagram without intending to. Half an hour later, I’m, like, ‘What am I still doing on this app?’ My average daily screen time is seven and a half hours. My relationship with my phone is not what I want it to be.”

The Offline Project is part of a new wave of digital detox communities that host events to give people time away from screens. It’s not hard to understand the appeal: adults in the UK now spend an average of four and a half hours online a day, and most of that is on their phones, according to Ofcom’s 2025 Online Nation report.

In 2025, the annual TouchPoints survey by the Institute of Practitioners in Advertising found that British adults were spending more time on their phones than watching TV for the first time. The government has recently announced that in spring 2027 it will bring in a social media ban for under-16s, which will include platforms like Instagram, TikTok and YouTube. When the news was announced, a teenage girl went viral when asked by a news reporter how she would spend all her newfound free time. Her answer? “Stare at a wall.”

Thankfully, if you want a break from your phone, there are plenty of things to do that are much more engaging. As our lives are becoming ever-more online, people are starting to push back against the hold that technology has on us. Sick of looking out at a sea of screens, some musicians are enforcing a no phones policy at their gigs. Bob Dylan’s 2025 UK and Ireland tour, Fred Again’s gigs at Alexandra Palace in February, and Harry Styles’s one-off gig in Manchester in March this year all had rules against using phones. It’s happening at comedy events, too – phones were placed in locked pouches at Sarah Silverman’s London Palladium gig last year, and Russell Howard’s current Don’t Tell the Algorithm tour promises “no phones, no distractions, just humans and jokes”.

According to data from Eventbrite, attendance at phone-free events in 2024 to 2025 increased by 121% globally. At broadcaster and DJ Annie Mac’s club night Before Midnight, stickers are placed on phone cameras so you can’t take photos or videos. “It reminds people to be in the moment. You’re only going to get so much satisfaction out of blurred videos with distorted sound, or dark, fuzzy photos,” she says. “Nightclubs are traditionally places where you go to feel a sense of freedom – to be whoever you want to be. They’re meant to be dark for that dual sense of losing yourself and finding yourself at the same time. Phones inhibit both of those things.”

While some are seeking out pockets of time at events and venues where they can escape their smartphones, others are going one step further and ditching them altogether. Cody Ramone, 31, from Derby, was using an old flip phone from 2015 until the pandemic, when life became more online than ever and he needed a smartphone again. In 2024, he switched back to a “dumb phone”. “I got tired of all the notifications and being constantly online,” he says.

Abandoning his smartphone has been transformative and given him time for more enriching activities. “I get bored more. Being bored is what drives you to try new things, pick up an old hobby, or think creatively. My attention span has improved, so I read more and spend more time doing creative hobbies, like crochet. I call people or hang out with them more often,” he says.

What is it that makes our phones so addictive? “Digital media activates the same reward pathway as drugs and alcohol, releasing dopamine, our reward neurotransmitter, in a key area of the reward pathway in the brain,” says Anna Lembke, professor of psychiatry at Stanford University School of Medicine and the author of Dopamine Nation. “Moving images are like catnip for the mammalian brain, leading to video-chaining, akin to ‘chain smoking’. Once we begin, it’s hard to stop, even when we want to.”

The more time we spend on our phones, the more we become “desensitised to what we are seeing” and look for more “potent rewards to recreate that original experience of pleasure”, says Lembke. “At the same time, we lose our ability to take joy in other more modest rewards, like watching a sunset, sharing a meal with friends, or reading a good book. We spend more time scrolling alone. We become increasingly dissatisfied and lonely.”

While that might sound like a bleak state of affairs, the good news is that it doesn’t have to be this way. With the rise of phone-free experiences, it’s possible to detach yourself from your device, even if it’s temporarily. “Part of having a healthier relationship with technology must include discrete periods of time when we are not using it, and instead fully present and interacting with the people and the world around us,” says Lembke. “This means creating collective spaces where we come together device-free.”

From off-grid, tech-free cabins to the pubs where devices aren’t allowed, these are the places to escape your phone in the UK.

Digital detox clubs

Set up in Amsterdam in 2024 by friends Jordy van Bennekom, Valentijn Klok and Ilya Kneppelhout, the Offline Club has 14 chapters in cities across 10 countries, including London and Bristol in the UK. Events start with everyone putting their devices in the “phone hotel”, a lockable metal box with slots. For the first hour, there’s music playing but no talking, and everyone does their own thing. For the second hour, people are encouraged to chat.

The demand for these kinds of events is growing. In London there’s the Switch Off – quiet, phone-free sessions for women where they can journal, collage or read a book – while the Offline Project hosts screen-free walks, talks and workshops. Logging Off Club is a UK initiative – with local groups in London, Bristol, Brighton, Southampton, Cambridge and the New Forest – that has now expanded to Sydney, Mexico City and Winnipeg.

In Bath, friends Nicola MacDonald and Laura Hughes started the Digital Detox Club in early 2025. They host events every two months at The Den cafe in Bath – phones go into the “tech motel” on arrival, and the pair provide optional activities like board games, journalling and crafts. “We’ve been struck by the diversity of attendees, from university students to retirees, which suggests this isn’t a niche concern,” says MacDonald. “It reflects a broader cultural fatigue with constant connectivity.”

If you’re trying to spend less time on your phone, a craft class does some of the work for you by keeping your hands busy. But there are specifically phone‑free classes, too. Native Hands offers basketry, pottery and bushcraft sessions, held outside in an ancient woodland in Sussex. At Curious House in East Sussex, classes range from basket weaving to portrait painting. All sessions start with a mindful breathing exercise to help people switch off.

In November last year, Dan Palmer launched Airplane Mode – a monthly phone-free event at his organic restaurant and natural wine bar, Eat Your Greens, in Leeds. The free events include workshops hosted by local creatives, doing things like painting, collage and origami.

Rather than locking phones away in a safe, they use a swear jar system. “Every time I catch anyone on their phone, I fine them 50p,” Palmer says. “All the fines go to a charity called Positive Action for Refugees and Asylum Seekers. So far, I’ve issued three fines – and one of them was for me! No one wants to be on their phones when they have something more interesting to do.”

The idea of using your hands to make something tangible rather than doomscrolling is what inspired Nadia Butt from Inner Canvas to host art sessions for women at her home in Reading without the distraction of screens. “The screen-free element is at the heart of the sessions,” she says. “We treat it like a ritual. At the start of each session, phones are silenced and placed in a box. I call it the ‘phone spa’. Framing it as something collective removes the anxiety around it.”

Spas are all about relaxing and switching off, but often these spaces aren’t phone-free. That is changing, though, with some spas now enforcing phone bans. The Bath Thermae Spa has a strict no phones policy – guests must put devices in a lockable pouch that’s kept in their locker. At Careys Manor in the New Forest, there’s a digital detox spa break, which includes relaxing treatments, a complimentary journal and a phone amnesty box in the room.

Phones have been banned at the Bothy at Heckfield Place, Hampshire, since it launched in 2023. “Seeing someone on their phone in a space dedicated to restoration felt out of alignment. You are there to be with yourself, to listen inwardly, to slow down,” says the spa operations director, Reka Seres-Erdei.

It’s not just at spas – as sauna culture rapidly grows, many people are finding these spaces offer a welcome break from technology. Ryan Haynes, 34, is a regular at London’s Community Sauna Baths, which has locations in Camberwell, Hackney Wick, Stratford, Walthamstow and Peckham. You can’t take your phone into the sauna, but you’re allowed to take photos outside, although they are considering a phone ban throughout.

Haynes’s Wednesday morning sauna session is “non-negotiable” for him. “All of my best ideas in the past two years have been while sitting in a sauna. Everyone needs to slow down to hear what’s going on in their brain,” he says.

As an independent bookshop owner and a sauna enthusiast, Kelly Wickson had an inspired idea last year: a book club in a sauna. Wickson owns Chapter 34 in Shoreham-by-Sea on the Sussex coast, and hosts the sauna book club once a month at the Nomadic Sauna on Kingston Beach. Creating a phone-free space was a big part of it, and the sauna conveniently ticks that box. “It will ruin your phone; you’ve got no choice,” she says.

The books are always 250 pages or less, and there’s no commitment to go every month. Phones are left in waterproof tubs outside the sauna. The book club is an hour long, and they go in and out of the sauna throughout, with some having a quick dip in the sea during breaks. Wickson has been amazed at how popular it is. “We do it on a Friday evening and it sells out,” she says.

While a book club in a sauna is particularly unusual, people increasingly value being given the time and space to switch off and read. This is the thinking behind Silent Book Club, where one of the mottoes is: “Put down your phone, pick up a book.” It’s a global network with about 2,000 chapters in more than 60 countries, and there are almost 150 in the UK and Ireland.

When Camille Jetzer and James Nasmyth opened the Roses of Elagabalus in Dalston, east London, last year, they knew they wanted to minimise phone use. They refer to it as a “clubhouse” – there’s a bar, restaurant, dancing and cabaret. “The idea of having no phones is that you would walk into the Roses, leave the outside world behind and enter this fantasy world where you can just enjoy the moment,” Jetzer says.

When you arrive at the Roses, a host explains that there’s no photography, and places a sticker over your phone camera. There are also reminders on the menus. “It’s a ‘you were there or you missed it’ situation,” Jetzer says, who has also noticed their regular punters reminding new visitors about the rule.

While phones aren’t locked away, Jetzer says the stickers on cameras mean they are used less. “It creates an environment where phones are less desired. In a dream world, we’d lock away the phones. That’s maybe next year’s project,” she says.

Elsewhere in London, Esmeralda’s Mayfair and the Spy Bar at Raffles London at the OWO both put stickers on phone cameras. In 2019, Samuel Smith’s pubs brought in a rule that customers couldn’t use phones or laptops in their establishments, of which there are more than 200 across the country. At the Barrel at Bude in Cornwall, anyone who breaks its no phones rule has to donate £1, which goes to local charities. In Herne Bay in Kent, the Butchers Arms has been a phone-free zone since it opened in 2005 – there are no signs needed to enforce it, says owner Martyn Hillier. “A disgruntled look from other customers is enough. If that doesn’t work we all start saying, ‘Rhubarb, rhubarb, rhubarb’, louder and louder until they realise they can’t converse any more.”

In Woking, Kim and Mike Jarred run Beyond the Screen, a monthly phone-free social at their local pub the Olive Tree. They set it up in March 2025 after talking about how they could model good phone habits for their teenage sons. They provide activities like puzzles and conversation starters, but mostly people just sit and chat. “Pubs are closing down and we’re just staying in our houses with our phones in front of our faces rather than getting out and meeting people. We’re human beings, and we need to connect with each other. Phones are getting in the way of that,” Kim says.

“Nights out now can feel like content creation exercises. We wanted to remove that layer entirely and return the focus to the room,” says James Hutchins, co-founder of Manchester club Amber’s. It opened in December 2024 and has a no-photo, no‑video policy, with stickers placed over phone cameras. “If people are seen taking photos or videos inside the club, they are politely asked to leave,” Hutchins says.

Amber’s is part of a growing trend in UK clubs, as more venues are making their dancefloors a phone‑free space. The policy is used at both Fold and Fabric in London, Lakota and sister venue Moon Club in Bristol, and Doppler Studio in Leicester. Some clubs ban phones completely. At Offgrid, a monthly day party at House Party in Soho, London, co‑founded by Stormzy, phones are sealed in a locked pouch. At her club night Before Midnight, Annie Mac has noticed a palpable shift in atmosphere – something she experienced during the first phone‑free Before Midnight event at the Warehouse Project in Manchester. “People were more present and louder. They whooped, they hollered, they whistled. They reacted to the tunes in a visceral way.”

In 2019, Hector Hughes was working for a tech startup in London and feeling burnt out. “I ended up at a silent retreat at a Buddhist temple on top of a mountain in the Himalayas. When you got there, they took your phone off you. I spent 10 days cut off from the outside world. It was a revelation,” says Hughes.

He came back from that trip, quit his job and started setting up Unplugged – off-grid cabins in the UK where you lock your phone away. It launched in the summer of 2020; there are now 60 digital detox cabins around the country (and they have expanded to Catalonia, too). The phone-free element is self‑policed, but each cabin has a lock box with a padlock, and the key is in a sealed envelope. They provide a Polaroid camera, a map and an old-school Nokia phone in case of emergencies. Hughes says that Unplugged’s customers often return for regular stays and go on to make changes in their daily lives, like having phone-free date nights or drastically cutting down their screen time.

If you like the idea of escaping to an off-grid cabin and ditching your phone, there are various options around the UK. Unyoked’s cabins run on solar power, have no wifi and often no phone signal – there’s a “spice signal”, from mild to extra spicy, to set expectations for how remote a cabin feels, and how long it might take to walk to one. They also have Brick devices, which help you block certain apps from your phone for a set amount of time. Similarly, Shacks’ cabins are off-grid with no wifi, and lockboxes for phones.

Alternatively, you could look for a remote cottage with no wifi and limited or no phone signal, like the Cottage in the Clouds in the middle of the Lake District national park, or Woodcock Cabin in the Cambrian mountains in Wales. If you want to escape dry land, too, Lilypod in Devon is a floating retreat with three solar-powered eco pods built on a platform next to a lake, where there’s no TV, wifi or phone signal, but there are board games, beanbags and a king-sized bed.

Florence Achery, founder of Yoga Retreats and More, launched her “Retreat like it’s 1999” digital detox breaks, in Lancashire and Cumbria, in 2023. A recent guest enjoyed the break from her devices so much that she forgot to pack her laptop and phone when she left. “I had to WhatsApp the guest she was travelling with to get them to pick up her stuff,” Achery says.

On arrival, guests hand over their devices before spending the next few days sharing meals together, going on long walks, doing yoga and star gazing. “They’re in charge, not their phones,” says Achery, who gives her guests a battery-powered alarm clock to take home, to encourage them to keep phones out of their bedrooms. She has also launched a parent and teen digital detox retreat to help younger people to change their relationship with technology.

At its 223-hectare (550-acre) estate on the River Dart in Devon, the Sharpham Trust hosts retreats focused on mindfulness and connecting to nature; guests are encouraged to switch off their phones.

EntertainmentTab.title: How Sam Fender and Olivia Dean's Rein Me In broke the UK's singles chart record
EntertainmentTab.text:
It's a song that has become inescapable, whether you're scrolling on TikTok, listening to the radio or even filling up your trolley on the weekly shop.

And now Rein Me In, the melodic love song by Sam Fender and Olivia Dean, has officially broken the longest standing record in British music history.

Speaking to Jack Saunders on BBC Radio 1's Official Chart show on Friday afternoon, Fender said he was "speechless" when asked how it felt to break the record.

By spending 19 non-consecutive weeks at the top of the UK singles chart, it overtakes the record set by American crooner Frankie Laine with his track I Believe, in 1953.

This reworking of Rein Me In, from Fender's third studio album, the Mercury Prize-winning People Watching, features an extra verse about the breakdown of a relationship from a female perspective, from Dean.

"[It's] very personal and reminded us of home, but when Olivia put her touch on it, it became a much more universal track," he told Radio 1, adding "that's what made it so huge and so beautiful".

He said he wanted to "personally thank" Dean, who helped him achieve his first ever number one single, adding: "It wouldn't have happened without Olivia obviously, but now I feel like it belongs to the fans, they've made it what it is".

When asked how he'd be celebrating the achievement, Fender joked "I think I'm just gonna have a really big sandwich".

It hasn't been a straightforward ascent to the top for Rein Me In - originally released as a solo Fender track and repurposed as a duet in June 2025, it took eight months to reach number one in February this year.

Dean said when the track came out, external that the original version of Rein Me In was her "favourite song on Sam's album" and it was "a pleasure to write a new verse from a female perspective".

A lot of the song's success as a duet comes from its authenticity, with the lyrics exploring the fallout from the end of a relationship and the difficulties faced by both parties as they try to move on from each other.

Whilst Fender's verses feel full of anger and regret at not being able to open up and be the partner he wanted to be, they are complimented by the softer and more reflective tone of Dean's, in which she encourages him to try again to make it work.

It has been described by Blunt Magazine's Jake Fitzpatrick, external as "stormy, tender and anthemic" and a "love letter to the kind of songwriting that knows when to burn slow".

The song has also received praise amongst many critics and bloggers, including Cult Following's Ewan Gleadow, external, who says that Dean's addition helps it to find "a new depth", noting "charm is a big part of it too, with all those reflections on where you come from and where you're headed".

Ben Mortimer, who runs Fender's label Polydor, described it as a "historic achievement" from "two homegrown stars" - Newcastle's Fender and London's Dean.

In an interview with Radio 1 when the track first hit number one, Fender acknowledged the track's slow climb to the top, thanking "the internet".

He also says he found it interesting that the track "travelled online and people came to it later, which is wonderful really because it's the music that's doing the talking".

The song has become a mainstay on TikTok - a quick scroll through the social media app shows its use on everything from grand declarations of love to montages of holidays and even compilations of football goals and celebrations.

It's also notable that the song first went viral after the pair performed it at a show at the London Stadium, home of Dean's team West Ham, in June last year.

She then returned the favour a week later at Newcastle United's St James Park, performing the song this time at the home of Fender's footballing love.

Whilst TikTok streams do not count towards the official charts, BBC research from last year explored how much of an effect the platform was having on what we listened to, particularly songs with meaningful and powerful lyrics.

EntertainmentTab.title: FLO say they 'want it all' after new album Therapy at the Club
EntertainmentTab.text:
"It's kind of been like a bit of a crash course in making music," says Stella Quaresma of making FLO's second album, Therapy at the Club.

After entering the music industry as teenagers, the British girl band say they grew to trust their own instincts during six months making their new record.

Formed of Quaresma, Jorja Douglas and Renée Downer, they first broke through in 2022 with the track Cardboard Box and have since won Best R&B/Soul Act at the 2026 MOBO Awards.

The group have more than five million monthly Spotify listeners and 1.2 million TikTok followers.

The campaign around their second album has included a NPR Tiny Desk performance viewed over a million times and appearances on high-profile US podcasts, helping reintroduce them stateside.

"It felt like we went to university and graduated with honours," Quaresma adds.

For their latest album, the group say they became more involved than ever before in every stage of the album's creation, from songwriting and vocal arrangements to production decisions.

"Sometimes you walk away from a session and people are surprised that you contributed, that you had ideas," says Douglas.

Quaresma suggests that's partly because when FLO first entered the industry, they leaned on the experience of the writers and producers around them.

"In the past we'd kind of been okay with that," she says. "But now we really don't need that kind of crutch."

For Downer, that greater creative control has resulted in FLO's most authentic record yet.

"We're definitely a lot more grown up. We've been a lot more involved, so this really is the best reflection of us at this point in time," she says.

Love has always been central to FLO's music, but on this album they explore its messier realities, with nights out providing the backdrop for stories of heartbreak, healing and friendship.

"So go ahead and kiss who you wanna / whatever the trauma / If you ever fall out of love / try therapy at the club," they sing on the title track.

Quaresma says the title came to represent the role friends can play during difficult moments.

"It's the idea that you're having the worst time of your life, but your friends are saying, 'No, you're coming out, you're going to dance and forget about it for a second.'"

While R&B remains at the heart of FLO's sound, they say they also aimed to push further into pop on their second album.

Quaresma says making Therapy at the Club taught her "how fun it is to really blend genres and to delve more into making pop music to make really big songs".

One example is Remedied, co-written with Grammy-winning songwriter Amy Allen, who has worked with pop stars Sabrina Carpenter and Tate McRae.

When making their Grammy-nominated debut album, Access All Areas, the FLO trio wrote songs together - but for Therapy at the Club, they wrote separately before bringing ideas back to one another.

Quaresma says this process helped them appreciate one another's strengths in a new way.

"You don't fully get to appreciate each other's talents when you're writing in a room of 10 people. To go away and write songs, then show each other what we'd made, was really special," she says.

That approach also extended to the album's collaborations. One of just two guest appearances on the record is Sex in Peace, their second collaboration with rising British R&B singer kwn. Quaresma wrote the song before bringing it to the rest of the group.

Downer says working with kwn has become a natural fit.

"We work really well with kwn when it comes to sexy R&B, so it felt right to send it to her and see if she'd do a verse," she says.

"She sent it back really quickly. We had no notes. We loved it."

EntertainmentTab.title: UK rapper Yung Filly found not guilty of raping woman after Australian show
EntertainmentTab.text:
UK rapper Yung Filly has been found not guilty of raping a fan after performing at a nightclub in Australia in 2024.

On Friday a jury in Western Australia found him not guilty for three counts of sexual penetration without consent.

But he was found guilty for two counts of assault occasioning bodily harm.

The YouTuber, whose real name is Andres Felipe Valencia Barrientos, had been accused of sexually assaulting the woman, then 20 years old, in his hotel room after he performed in Hillarys, a coastal suburb of Perth.

The jury could not come to a decision on three other counts of rape.

Barrientos was also found not guilty for one count of assault occasioning bodily harm and also for strangulation.

The 30-year-old social media star, who pleaded not guilty to all charges, cried when the verdict was read out, local media reported.

He will remain on bail until 21 August, when the court will decide his sentencing date.

Prosecutors will also decide on the next steps for the three hung jury verdicts - whether to press ahead or not on those rape charges.

Barrientos has been on bail since being charged and was allowed to fly home to the UK in September for four months, before returning to Western Australia ahead of his trial.

During the trial, Barrientos had told the court that he had "fancied" the woman when they met at the concert venue.

Barrientos, who was born in Colombia and brought up in the UK, had been in the VIP area while she leaned over the barrier from the general area.

He denied touching her inappropriately.

"I recall putting my hand on her waist," he told the court. But he said he had not put his hands down her pants or touched her breast.

He said the "vibes were good" between him and the woman when they arrived at his hotel later.

His security guard took the woman's phone away - "standard practice" to protect their privacy, according to Barrientos.

The court heard that the pair had engaged in consensual sex in his hotel room before Barrientos turned violent and the young woman, who cannot be named for legal reasons, told him to stop.

The woman accused the social media star of biting, bruising and even trying to choke her. Photos of bruises and bite marks on her face and neck were shown in court.

Barrientos denied the woman had repeatedly asked him to stop, but did acknowledge that he bit her several times, explaining that he gave her a "love bite".

During the trial's closing arguments, prosecutor Danielle Clarke said Barrientos was an "entitled" man with a "moderate degree of fame" who had violated the fan "in the most intrusive way possible".

His defence lawyer argued that the accuser's evidence was full of "inconsistencies, embellishments and outright lies".

Barrientos is known for his work with the YouTube collective Beta Squad, and has appeared in the celebrity version of Bake Off on Channel 4 and presented BBC Three shows.

In addition to his 1.8 million YouTube subscribers, he has three million followers on TikTok and and 2.4 million on Instagram.

EntertainmentTab.title: Glasgow gets starring role in Spider-Man: Brand New Day film
EntertainmentTab.text:
Any comic book fan knows that Spider-Man's secret identity is Peter Parker, a science nerd who gained superhero powers after being bitten by a radioactive spider.

But in the latest installment from the Marvel cinematic universe, Spider-Man: Brand New Day, Parker - played by Tom Holland - is not the only star in disguise.

The action takes place in New York City but much of the movie, which premiered in London this week, was filmed more than 3,000 miles away in Glasgow.

Filming almost brought the city centre to a halt last summer, when fans gathered to watch Holland in an action sequence in full superhero mode.

Parts of the nearby Merchant City were also dressed up to resemble the Big Apple.

It was the latest in a long line of Hollywood blockbusters to have been filmed in the city in recent years.

And next month Glasgow is expected to double as Gotham City, when filming starts on the sequel to The Batman.

Screen Scotland said the Victorian architecture, wide avenues and grid layout make it an "incredibly versatile stand-in" for many US cities.

Filmmaker Destin Daniel Cretton praised Scotland as a filming destination during an interview at the premiere on Wednesday.

"I love Scotland," he told Press Association.

"I got to go to Scotland first ages ago with a short film to the Edinburgh Film Festival and I fell in love with that place."

The 37-year-old added: "When we shot in Glasgow, that was our first day shooting and that was just such an energising way to start.

"We had thousands of people show up who are cheering us on and getting excited and feeling that energy which was really a wonderful way to start."

Screen Scotland, which supports Scotland's film and TV industry, said: "It's fantastic to see Spiderman: Brand New Day hitting our screens.

"As we can already see from the trailer, Glasgow has a starring role, as the city once again seamlessly doubles for New York.

"Glasgow's grid layout, wide avenues and Victorian architecture make it an incredibly versatile stand-in for many US cities including New York and Philadelphia and Spiderman: Brand New Day is the latest example of the scale of production the city can accommodate."

EntertainmentTab.title: What your summer reading list says about you
EntertainmentTab.text:
You've been dreaming about that summer break on the sun lounger, book in one hand and drink in the other, for months. Now the dash to the airport gate, train station or hours-long drive is all that stands in your way.

But what does the book you've just shoved in your suitcase say about you?

"It's definitely not a random choice," says Edgar Dubourg, a cognitive scientist at the École Normale Supérieure in Paris. "Your reading list is basically a map of your personality.

"When you pick a thriller or romance or horror or science fiction you're not escaping your psychology, in a way, you're really feeling very intuitive and very old parts of your brain.

"Fiction isn't inventing new emotions in you. It's pressing on those pre-existing motivations like instincts."

Studies have shown that our book choices can subconsciously reveal important parts of our personality - including what gives us pleasure and what makes us feel emotion.

Research by Dr Valerie van Mulukom, a senior lecturer in psychology at Oxford Brookes University, suggests that our inner anxieties (or what she calls existential insecurities) determine which book we pick from the shelf.

During her study, she used how often someone might engage with a certain genre to match it up with one of the following four clusters:

But what do they mean? And how do they match up with our own anxieties?

EntertainmentTab.title: Tyla world tour: Nigeria removed from South African singer's itinerary
EntertainmentTab.text:
Just days after South African singer Tyla released the dates for her upcoming world tour, Nigeria has been removed from the list of destinations.

On Monday, the Grammy winner announced details of her globetrotting appearances coming on the heels of the release of her second album A*POP.

Her official website initially named 34 cities, including Lagos, Johannesburg and Cape Town, where she would be performing, but by Friday, an updated list was published without the Nigerian city.

No reason has been given for the change but there have been growing calls in Nigeria for the 24-year-old to cancel her concert in the country over the recent wave of anti-migrant sentiment in South Africa.

Relations between Nigeria and South Africa have soured over allegations that Nigerians have been the target of xenophobic violence.

Nigeria, along with other African countries, has accused South Africa of not doing enough to deal with attacks on foreign nationals.

There have also been a series of protests with people calling for all undocumented migrants to leave South Africa. Tens of thousands of foreigners have left the country, including Nigerians, many of whom boarded specially chartered repatriation flights.

While there have been diplomatic efforts to calm tensions, most recently with a meeting between their foreign affairs officials in Abuja, the issue has spread beyond politics.

On Wednesday, an online petition titled "Ban Tyla from entering Nigeria until xenophobic attacks stop in South Africa" was launched in Nigeria and it has already attracted thousands of signatures.

On Tyla's social media pages, where the initial tour dates still appear, Nigerians cautioned her against performing in the country as they criticised her for failing to speak out against the protests in South Africa.

Tyla has so far not responded to a BBC request for comment.

Tyla is not the only South African artist facing a backlash for their seeming silence on the anti-migrant protests.

Comedian Trevor Noah also came under fire following an advert he fronted for the Tourism Business Council of South Africa.

The promotional clip, shared across the council's various social media accounts, generated many comments criticising the former Daily Show host for promoting South Africa but failing to call out xenophobic attitudes.

Users even went as far as to add context under the video saying South Africa was "a xenophobic country [that] doesn't allow visiting migrants".

The backlash has extended beyond criticism; some South African artists have reportedly lost out on performances across the continent.

South Africa's Justice Minister Mmamoloko Kubayi said in June that a local artist had told her that "all her gigs were cancelled". The minister did not name the artist.

"So the [South Africa] brand does get affected," she said at the time.

The South African government has also pushed back on the growing wave of criticism.

It says that it does deal with anyone who takes the law into their own hands, pointing out that more than 900 people were arrested after recent protests, but that it has a right to control migration into the country.

The online debate around Tyla's world tour has opened a much wider conversation on whether African artists be held responsible for the political tensions between their countries.

Nigerian activist, opposition politician and former presidential candidate Omoyele Sowore said on X that anger over anti-migrant attacks should be directed at political leaders in Nigeria and South Africa, rather than artists.

In a post, he said: "No-one should hold a talented musician like Tyla vicariously liable for the crimes of xenophobia. Artistes are not responsible for the failures of politicians except where there is ample evidence they're enablers."

Nigerian culture journalist Mayowa Idowu told the BBC that while the anger may come from a desire for accountability, directing it towards an artist risks missing the wider issue.

"I think they are well intentioned because people are seeking accountability and they're looking beyond governments who they do not trust or have faith in. That said, I think they are misguided and they risk devolving into acts of hypocrisy. The artist in question has worked with Nigerian artists and performed in Nigeria previously," he said.

Idowu argues that performers should not be pressured into taking political positions simply because of their nationality.

Tyla has found herself at the centre of rivalry between the two countries before.

Earlier this year, she beat four other African artists, including three from Nigeria, to clinch her second Grammy award in the Best African Music Performance category.

She won the inaugural version of the prize in 2024, again beating a field that included Nigerian heavyweights such as Burna Boy and Davido.

With two wins in the category's first three years, Tyla has become one of the biggest Grammy success stories in African music - while also becoming a symbol in a fan rivalry that often frames Nigerian and South African artists against each other.

UK-based Nigerian culture journalist and writer Dami Ajayi said that Tyla has never presented herself to be anti-Nigeria but "we interpret her winning two Grammy Awards in a nominations list full of Nigerian musicians as being anti-Nigerian".

"These targeted retaliatory campaigns are not particularly new. There were also calls to boycott the recent hit Netflix show The Polygamist, adapted from Zimbabwean Sue Nyathi's novel and co-directed by Akin Omotosho, a Nigerian living in South Africa," he added.

South African journalist Thango Ntwasa said that while it was difficult to comment on the removal of Lagos from Tyla's world tour line-up, "it's a very interesting time because we're seeing arts and politics... really confronting each other now more than ever".

He also touched on the criticism levelled at artists like Tyla and Noah on their apparent silence on the migration issue, saying that while it's understandable for artists to want to be apolitical, it was important for "celebrities... to understand that as a public figure, your opinion or position on a political issue does matter".

Ntwasa noted that South African artists had reported facing animosity when visiting other African nations and that, because touring is a big part of how they make money, the negative attitudes could affect them down the line.

EntertainmentTab.title: Sarn artist Kevin Sinnott dies aged 78
EntertainmentTab.text:
One of Wales' leading contemporary artists has died at the age of 78.

Kevin Sinnott who was born in Sarn, Bridgend county, to Irish parents, rose to fame for his painting Running Away with the Hairdresser.

The famous work of art, which portrays two figures running along a terraced street, can be seen at the National Museum in Cardiff.

Museum Wales said Sinnott was one of Wales' most acclaimed painters, with his work held in major collections in the UK and internationally.

Trained at the Royal College of Art in London, Sinnott enjoyed great success in the 1980s with exhibitions at prominent galleries in London and the United States.

His work was acquired by the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York, the British Council, the Royal College of Art in London, the British Museum, and Amgueddfa Cymru – Museum Wales.

He continued painting at his home in the Garw Valley until the end of his life.

His wife Susan died in 2017 and he is survived by his four children and 11 grandchildren.

EntertainmentTab.title: Mahrajan Festival in London is a 'milestone' for Arabic community
EntertainmentTab.text:
Some of the biggest Arabic artists in the world are descending on the UK on Saturday - for a "first of its kind" music festival.

Mahrajan Festival is an entirely Arabic music event and fans have been telling BBC Newsbeat they are ready to "enjoy and celebrate" the milestone.

Organised as a collaboration between Live Nation and ABU Recordings, the event has been billed as a platform to "honour Arabic music across all generations".

Egyptian singer Lella Fadda says she's "super excited" to be one of the performers taking to the stage.

The all-day outdoor festival is taking place at Crystal Palace Bowl and includes a mix of established artists as well as rising stars.

"I have never performed here before - when I perform abroad most of the people don't know me so they get to know me through the performance which I really love," says Lella.

The artist is vocally trained but says she has always loved rap, which is how she got into it.

"Not everyone knows me at the [festival] because I rap in mostly Egyptian Arabic and it's not for all the diaspora to understand, but I'm so happy to be connecting with everyone."

The likes of Saint Levant, Dystinct and Khaled are headlining the one-day festival, which feels like a step forward for Arabic music fan Mariam Azam.

"Growing up we didn't see ourselves in the media at all, and if we did it was never good representation," the 24-year-old says.

"It's just nice to have something for us, especially in London."

Azam says she has been "counting down the days" until the festival - and she's not the only one who's excited.

Natalina Popat tells Newsbeat she's most looking forward to seeing Palestinian artist Saint Levant.

"I'm really hoping that he plays Samra, which is a song about loving a girl with a little bit of a darker skin tone," says the 25-year-old.

"I think in a community where fair is often the more beautiful, that song is really comforting and I love it a lot."

Popat grew up in Dubai and Saudi Arabia and says she was "always surrounded by the culture".

"I feel like I was very blessed to have a lot of my childhood kind of mixed in with that community."

When she moved to the UK, she felt a shift.

"There wasn't as much [Arab music] in the mainstream media, so that's why I'm excited for this festival to meet like-minded people.

"And also have a chance to enjoy and celebrate this milestone in the Arab community."

EntertainmentTab.title: Zendaya and Tom Holland: Their decade-long Spider-Man romance in pictures
EntertainmentTab.text:
Newlyweds Tom Holland and Zendaya stepped out together on Wednesday to promote their fourth Spider-Man film together.

Over the course of a decade we have seen them grow up together on the big screen.

Let's spin a web back to the past and compare how they were when their spider-senses first started tingling together, to now.

Holland and Zendaya were just 20 and 19 years old, respectively, when they first met in 2016 on the set of Spider-Man: Homecoming, during the movie's casting and initial production.

The film showed British actor Holland as Peter Parker balancing high school life with being a superhero - Spider-Man - for the first time.

It also introduced US actress Zendaya as Michelle Jones-Watson - aka MJ - his awkward but intellectual classmate.

The on-screen chemistry was clear from the start and the film received good reviews but the pair denied rumours of a romance, insisting they were just close friends while promoting the movie.

They even took to Twitter [now X] to make light of the rumours. She posted: "Wait wait ... my favourite is when it says we go on vacations together HA! I haven't been on a vacation in years! hbu @TomHolland1996 ???"

Holland responded: "Does the press tour count?"

The pair continued to film and promote Marvel projects together.

They were back on the red carpet together in 2019 for the release of Spider-Man: Far From Home.

The movie saw Peter go on a school trip to Europe, where he teamed up with MJ.

It also saw them share their first on-screen kiss as their characters grew closer.

In summer 2021, the acting pair were photographed embracing in Los Angeles in real life, driving fans online wild.

Later that year, they were looking cosy on the campaign trail for Spider-Man: No Way Home, which also saw Zendaya's famous method dressing in her spider-webbed outfit.

Their third Spider-Man film together saw multiverse chaos break out after Peter's identity is revealed, with MJ by his side.

A few months after the premiere, Holland marked Zendaya's birthday by posting a selfie from the set, alongside the caption: "My MJ, have the happiest of birthdays. Gimme a call when your up xxx."

Soon after, Hollywood's hottest couple appeared together on the red carpet for Wednesday's London premiere of their fourth Spider-Man story, which picks up years after the events of No Way Home in a world where no-one remembers Peter.

On working with her husband, Zendaya, 29, told BBC News: "When you're best friends, it's easy."

Tomdaya, as they are affectionately known online, are featuring together in another new film, The Odyssey, but for Spider-Man fans, at least, they will be Peter and MJ forever.

EntertainmentTab.title: 'Surreal' moment as Welsh actor Rex Hayes joins Ted Lasso cast
EntertainmentTab.text:
Rex Hayes has been watching hit comedy series Ted Lasso since it first landed on TV screens in 2020.

But now the Cardiff actor is stepping on to "that pitch, in those football boots" as the show returns for a new season.

"It's very surreal for me to be part of that Richmond world," the actor tells Radio Wales.

Season 4 marks a dramatic shift for the show, with Ted returning from Kansas to coach AFC Richmond's second-division women's team, The Lady Greyhounds.

"It's exactly the same set-up: you meet new people, you fall in love with these characters on, and off, the pitch. There's all the coaching staff that you know and love, but with brand-new footballers," says Rex. "It's very exciting."

Joining a cast which includes fan favourites Hannah Waddington, Brett Goldstein and star and co-creator Jason Sudeikis, Rex plays Siobhan, twin sister to Niamh (Aisling Sharkey), whose sibling rivalry sometimes spills on to the pitch.

"I love this character so much - I can't wait for people to meet her," Rex tells Eleri Sion on The Friday Afternoon Show. "She's very passionate, very silly."

A keen footballer from a young age, Rex describes the role as "a crazy matching of both my worlds".

"I have been playing football for most of my life," explains Rex. "Just me and my dad, at Heath Park, kicking a ball about, for most of my youth.

"I played in the school yard every lunchtime until my A levels - me and the boys. It's been a big part of my life for a long time."

But after giving up football training at 12, the actor "went off to drama school and forgot about it" - only returning to the pitch after moving to London.

Cue, the Ted Lasso audition.

"I had to send in a tape of my football skills," says Rex, who made a tape in a London park.

"I remember when I went in for my first meeting, having sent off that tape, Theo - the casting director - was like, 'you're very good at football'. I was like: 'yes, I am - remember that!"

"And lo and behold, here I am. So I'm very grateful."

Rex credits their early years performing in Wales as fundamental to later success.

"I am under no illusion that going to a Welsh-language school, and being part of the Eisteddfod for most of my youth, is a big part of the reason why I now do the job that I do," says the actor.

"I am incredibly grateful to the Welsh language, to S4C, and to the Eisteddfod for all of those opportunities.

"It gave me a platform and taught me a lot of what I know, and what I have taken on for the rest of my career."

This weekend Rex will be returning to this year's Eisteddfod, in Llantwd (Llandudoch), north Pembrokeshire, to support their mum.

"My mam is singing, and this is my first time getting to watch her.

"It's a lovely passing of the baton - after all the hours that she put in when I was a kid, watching me on that stage. I will be down [in Wales] and I really can't wait."

Sadly, though, we won't be hearing any Welsh in Ted Lasso.

"You won't meet me with a Welsh accent - my character is Irish," says Rex.

Nonetheless, the actor hopes fans will embrace the show's new female football team.

"I would ask audiences to meet us [the new cast] the same way you met the men's team - with open hearts, in the way that Ted Lasso meets everyone.

"One of my favourite quotes from the show is: 'be curious, not judgemental'. That's my ethos for anyone meeting the show this season."

"It's such a privilege to be a part of something like this," adds Rex, reflecting on the support shown by regulars such as Waddington and Sudeikis to the new cast.

"These people have been doing this for a long time, and have really honed their craft. They know what it takes to be good people, both on set and off.

"I've learnt a lot from them, and from my new colleagues."

The Lady Greyhounds include Game of Thrones' Faye Marsay, Abbie Hern, Jude Mack and Tanya Reynolds, as well as Rex's screen sister Sharkey.

"We are best mates. What you see on screen is very much our real life relationship, we adore each other. I can't wait for the world to meet all of them," says Rex.

"Trying on that kit for the first time, wearing that badge that I had fallen in love with... and then stepping out on that pitch, in those football boots, pretending to be a football player - all of it - I will never take it for granted, for sure."

The new series lands on Apple TV+ on 5 August.

EntertainmentTab.title: Former England football star Shaun Wright-Phillips joins Strictly 2026 line-up
EntertainmentTab.text:
Former England and Manchester City winger Shaun Wright-Phillips is the latest star to join the line-up for this year's Strictly Come Dancing.

The football pundit, who is the son of Arsenal legend Ian Wright, had 36 caps for England and also played for clubs including Chelsea and Queens Park Rangers.

His fancy footwork may have dazzled on the pitch but Wright-Phillips says this latest challenge "is definitely outside my comfort zone. Dancing is in my blood -but mainly at family events! I'm super excited to get started and really looking forward to the challenge!"

While ex-footballers have had mixed fortunes on previous Strictly series, former soccer star Karen Carney flipped the script last year by winning the coveted glitterball.

Wright-Phillips is the tenth celebrity to be confirmed for this year's series, joining stars including Delta Goodrem, Lacey Turner, Dani Dyer and Jaime Winstone.

More celebrities are set to be announced in the coming weeks, with 15 expected in the final line-up.

Scroll down to see the rest of this year's line-up so far:

Antonia has portrayed dragon-rider Lady Baela Targaryen in HBO's Game of Thrones prequel since 2022. She is currently starring as Eurydice in the Tony Award-winning musical Hadestown in London's West End.

Her acting career began when she was 14 when she appeared in a short film adaptation of The Tempest, before being cast as a guest role in the BBC's Doctors.

The singer and actress has also appeared in series including Nolly, Stay Close, Stath Lets Flats, and Doctor Who.

Antonia said: "I can't quite believe that I will be heading to the Strictly ballroom this September! I have grown up watching Strictly, and I am so excited to take the challenge on and (hopefully!) learn a new skill. See you on the dancefloor!"

Jaime Winstone launched her acting career in 2004 and her film credits include Bullet Boy, Tomb Raider and Wild Bill, as well stage productions such as 2:22 A Ghost Story.

The actress, who also won acclaim for her portrayal of Barbara Windsor in the BBC biopic Babs, said she was "so excited" to be joining the dance competition.

The actress said in a statement she was "no stranger to a dance floor", but added that ballroom is "a whole new world for me".

"I love a challenge though," she continued, "so can't wait to enter my showgirl era and get super sparkly!"

Winstone has also appeared in TV series such as Poirot, Dead Set, Torvill & Dean, Mad Dogs, Count Abdulla and Four Lives.

After playing Windsor in Babs, Winstone stepped into the late actress's famous role of Peggy Mitchell in EastEnders, appearing in flashback specials, most recently in the soap's 40th anniversary last year.

Known as Great Britain's most successful Paralympian of all time, Dame Sarah Storey has secured 19 gold medals across the nine Paralympic Games she competed in.

The swimmer and cyclist said embarking on the challenge is "hugely exciting" and she "can't wait to get started".

"I have always loved watching Strictly and my daughter Louisa is a very talented dancer, so to be able to learn from the best and hopefully understand even more about her world, is incredibly motivating!" she said.

The former athlete won four golds at London 2012. She started her career as a swimmer and later switched to cycling, winning 30 Paralympic medals in total.

Best is known for hosting Big Brother with AJ Odudu on ITV since 2023, and as host of the Hits Radio Breakfast Show alongside Fleur East and James Barr.

He said it was "an absolute dream" to be taking to the BBC One contest's dance floor in September, "albeit a pretty terrifying one".

Best added: "I've been lucky to do lots of live telly before, but absolutely nothing like this. And I cannot wait!

"I have no idea if I can actually dance, but bring on the sequins, bring on the quicksteps, bring on the dance floor! I'm going to try to enjoy every minute of it."

Mercer was part of the winning couple on ITV dating show Love Island last year, and also works as a model and DJ, and is an ambassador for a young people's mental health charity.

"I have grown up watching the show with my family and am so excited to now be part of the cast," he said.

Mercer also showcases his Afrobeat, hip-hop and street dance moves on his social media accounts.

"Dancing is a huge passion of mine and I can't wait to learn ballroom and do the foxtrot for the first time!" he added.

Delta Goodrem is also part of this year's celebrity list, with the Australian singer and actress becoming the third celebrity to be announced for the upcoming series.

"I've been incredibly honoured to perform on many different stages throughout my career - from TV, theatre, film sets, to touring my own shows around the world," Goodrem said.

"There is, however, one stage I've never stepped onto and that is the ballroom floor. I'm absolutely thrilled to be joining Strictly and can't wait to get started."

She rose to fame in hit Australian soap opera Neighbours and recently represented her nation in the 2026 edition of the Eurovision Song Contest.

Celebrity hair stylist Chris Appleton is also part of this year's line-up.

Appleton, best known for his work with Kim Kardashian, joins singer-songwriter Delta Goodrem, EastEnders actress Lacey Turner and reality star Dani Dyer in the battle for the Glitterball trophy.

The Leicester-born Color Wow creative director said: "I'm thrilled to be joining Strictly Come Dancing and coming home to the UK for this incredible experience."

He has also created red carpet looks for the likes of Jennifer Lopez, Katy Perry and Ariana Grande, while having his work showcased on the covers of publications including Vogue, Harper's Bazaar and Vanity Fair.

"I've always believed that the best things happen when you take a chance and try something new," added the 43-year-old, who this year released a memoir entitled Your Roots Don't Define You.

"I may know my way around a salon floor, but the dance floor is a whole different story - and I can't wait to get started."

Lacey Turner was the first contestant to be announced for this year's series, which is expected to begin in September.

She said she was "so excited to be making my way to the dance floor", adding that she was a "huge fan" of the show.

Turner, 38, is best known for her role as Stacey Slater on the BBC One soap, which she joined in 2004.

She has won a British Soap Award and National Television Award for her role, and has also starred in TV dramas including the BBC's Our Girl.

In a video posted on Instagram, Turner said she was "so excited and so terrified at the same time" to be taking part in the show.

"But I've had so many friends do Strictly, and I thought it was about time that I pluck up the courage and made my way on to the dance floor."

Josh Widdicombe, Emma Willis and Johannes Radebe will take over as Strictly presenters this year, following the departures of Tess Daly and Claudia Winkleman.

The first line-up announcements were made significantly earlier than usual - the BBC usually confirms the line-up in August.

Speaking to ITV's Good Morning Britain in June, Ballas said: "There are going to be some people on there that will make you go 'wow'."

Asked about the new presenting trio, Ballas said she was "very excited to see what they bring" to the show.

"I know they took lots of chemistry tests, as did everybody, and those chemistry tests have brought those three people together, and I believe it's absolutely unbelievable," she said.

Ballas described the number of new elements on this year's show as "quite extraordinary", but added that it will still feel familiar to viewers.

"I don't think they'll change the show too much, maybe tweaks here and there, but no major changes."

Ballas, Craig Revel Horwood, Motsi Mabuse and Anton Du Beke will all return as judges.

Regular pro dancers including Amy Dowden, Dianne Buswell, Katya Jones, Vito Coppola and Aljaz Skorjanec will all be back on the dance floor.

However, professional dancers Gorka Marquez, Nadiya Bychkova, Luba Mushtuk, Karen Hauer and Michelle Tsiakkas will not be returning this year.

EntertainmentTab.title: BTS are back: return of K-pop superstars sparks US economic boom
EntertainmentTab.text:
BTS’s “Army” fanbase is descending on New York this weekend as the K-pop supergroup continues their first world tour after a four-year hiatus, sparking an economic boom wherever they land.

After shows in South Korea and Europe, the group are back in North America, with 14 shows in six US cities in August and September.

Following the rollout of BTS’s sixth album, Arirang, in March, fans have proved they are willing to spend. In Las Vegas, concertgoers who attended four sold-out shows in May generated an estimated $340m in economic activity, with events at huge hotels on the strip and at tiny Chinatown cafes.

HYBE, the group’s label, has partnered with local businesses and cultural centers for the “BTS The City – Arirang” project in select cities, offering exclusive BTS programming for concertgoers.

Ahead of two concerts at New Jersey’s MetLife Stadium on 1 and 2 August, fans can follow a map of activities, landmarks and eateries that celebrate the group.

Manhattan’s Koreatown is bracing for thousands of fans. The economic impact of BTS concertgoers is expected to match that of soccer fans who crowded MetLife Stadium for the World Cup final – which included a BTS performance – a few weeks ago.

BTS will “easily compare [to] or even exceed Fifa’s economic impact just on average spending”, said Michael Mariano, head of economic development at Tourism Economics.

The group’s return has been a boon for HYBE, which reported a record-high revenue of $993m this past quarter.

The Korean Cultural Center New York will serve as the hub for fan activities. Participants who nabbed a coveted reservation can try on K-beauty products, sample desserts from Tous les Jours, a South Korean bakery chain, and customize the light sticks they’ll bring to the concert, known as “Army bombs”.

“K-pop can serve as a gateway to learning the Korean language and discovering Korean beauty, food, technology, tourism and other aspects of Korean culture,” said Bora Yoon, visual arts manager at the center.

The Arte Museum, which houses large-scale digital art, is hosting a special BTS exhibit that will feature music and digital art celebrating the group’s music. The museum expects a high demand for the exhibit, which will immerse BTS fans in “all five senses”, said Sang Jin Lee, head of the creative team and vice-president of d’strict, a creative design company that owns the Arte Museum.

“It’s about sharing our culture, great heritage and Korean contemporary digital art through the lens of BTS, using an enduring folk song that is continually reinterpreted by every generation,” Lee said in Korean, referring to Arirang, the centuries-old folk song that inspired the name of BTS’s new album.

New Wonjo, the oldest Korean barbecue restaurant in New York, is also featured on the map, and plans to serve a special menu inspired by the members of BTS and the foods they miss most on tour, including kimchi fried rice, pork belly and jajangmyeon, or black bean noodles.

The menu was developed “with intention, and is rooted in Korean culture, rather than just pasting ‘BTS’ on a regular menu item”, said Jacob Baik, art director of New Wonjo. “We hope that some guests who might initially visit because of the ‘BTS The City’ project leave with a genuine interest in the restaurant, the food and Korean culture more broadly.”

The map also features bingsu, a type of South Korean shaved ice dessert, offered by Seoul Bingsu – a pop-up version of Seoul-based Tokyo Bingsu, known for its tomato flavor of the dessert. For its limited 10-day New York run, Seoul Bingsu will offer special bookmarks, pins and stickers for those who order from its special Arirang menu.

Ara Go, the Seoul-based owner of Seoul Bingsu, said BTS “has truly helped introduce Korean culture to the world”.

“Food and desserts are a huge part of Korean culture, and I saw this as a wonderful opportunity to promote not only our food but our country with a broader audience,” Go said in Korean.

Before the spot’s collaboration with BTS, Angela May, 18, had never heard of bingsu. May, a BTS fan for nearly six years, traveled to Manhattan from New Jersey to try it.

“Just having BTS written on the menu or the window will bring a lot of attention to the place,” May said.

Asli Penaeo, 22, grew up in New York and has been a fan for seven years, yet she has never been to most of the collaborating restaurants.

“This event is finally giving me a chance to go to some of these restaurants, try new items, but also make new memories with fellow Army [fans],” she said, sipping on a BTS-branded Tous Les Jours strawberry lemonade.

Sunmi Lee, 40, an interior designer, said she was considering taking a BTS-themed double-decker bus tour to visit New York landmarks – even though she lives in the city.

“It’s about celebrating Korean culture,” she said. “Trying authentic local spots, and feeling connected to something bigger than just a concert.”

GeneralTab.title: Spain attacks 'selfish' response of some EU countries to Ceuta migrant crossings
GeneralTab.text:
Spain has condemned the "selfish, polarising and unlawful" reaction of some EU countries to the influx of about 60,000 migrants from Morocco to Ceuta.

Officials say almost all those who reached the enclave on 30 July have returned, while Spain's Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska said on Saturday that the death toll had risen to at least 67.

It comes after Italy temporarily suspended the EU's border-free Schengen arrangement with Spain, as Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni called the scenes "shocking".

Finland and Denmark backed Italy's move, while Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš urged a temporary suspension of Spain's Schengen membership.

In a letter to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said he had "serious concerns" about some European governments.

He said the Spanish government had fully restored control over the border and prevented any "unauthorised onward movement towards continental Europe" in less than 48 hours.

While most had shown "support and solidarity", Sanchez said other European governments had chosen to attack Spain, "driven by prejudice, fake news, ignorance, or political interest", and pointed out that Ceuta was not part of the Schengen area.

"The European Union cannot afford this kind of selfish, polarising and unlawful reaction," he said.

The Spanish leader called for an urgent meeting with EU interior ministers to "reaffirm that the security of our external borders is a shared responsibility of all Member States".

Meanwhile, 22 of the EU's 27 countries also called for emergency talks in an open letter, citing "serious concerns" regarding the developments in Ceuta.

The nations "welcome that Spain and Morocco are cooperating closely to ensure the swift return of migrants", but said a video conference of EU interior ministers would help reach agreement on mobilising EU instruments and support for Spain to restore "effective control" of the border and prevent further uncontrolled crossings.

Also on Saturday, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he had spoken to Sánchez and the UK was "providing what help we can".

But while the situation on the ground appears to be easing, political and diplomatic fallout is rippling through Madrid and other capitals.

On Thursday, Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni wrote on social media that such "uncontrolled immigration" was a threat to national security, before suspending the Schengen zone agreement with Spain for a month.

The Schengen Area is a system of open borders spanning 29 European countries that have abolished controls at their common borders.

Spain responded by summoning the Italian ambassador to Madrid, while its foreign minister said he expected "European solidarity and not partisan demagoguery".

Finland's Interior Minister Mari Rantanen said she had started preparations for restoring internal border checks "if the need arises". She also urged "all European countries" to support Meloni's move.

Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen also urged the EU to "consider all options, including a suspension of Schengen co-operation".

France has tightened checks on its border with Spain and said it would increase its police presence by Saturday.

Portuguese PM Luis Montenegro said he was considering reinforcing border checks.

Von der Leyen said the images from Ceuta were "unacceptable". "We cannot allow anyone to come to our Union without abiding by our rules," she said on social media.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said he "supports Spain's intention not to allow illegal migrants onto the European continent", and demanded that Morocco "take back illegal migrants immediately".

In the US, the State Department said the incident was a direct result of Spain's migration policies. President Donald Trump called the situation a "catastrophe" and said "it looks like an invasion of a country by hundreds of thousands of people".

Morocco, which has been suffering from a high unemployment rate, witnessed several Gen Z anti-government protests last year, with young people demanding better opportunities and improvements to public services.

Together with Melilla, Ceuta forms the European Union's only land borders with Africa. Migrants can enter the enclave by swimming several kilometres.

Spain has a relatively friendly approach to immigration. In April, the government approved plans to give legal status to 500,000 undocumented migrants, allowing them to be formally integrated into the workforce.

At that time, the right-wing Italian prime minister had already criticised Sánchez, saying the policy would "affect its neighbours".

In June the European Parliament approved tougher migration rules that grant authorities broader powers to return irregular arrivals.

GeneralTab.title: Mountaineer Nirmal Purja killed in Pakistan avalanche, his company says
GeneralTab.text:
Renowned mountaineer and former British Army soldier Nirmal Purja is among those killed in an avalanche on Broad Peak in Pakistan, his company has said.

Sharing the news on social media, Elite Expeditions said it confirmed with "profound sadness and immense heartbreak" that Purja had died in Thursday's avalanche.

It also said that none of other nine members of the expedition had survived.

Purja, a Nepali-born climber, was known for scaling the world's 14 highest peaks in just over six months in 2019.

Pakistani officials had previously announced that the bodies of three climbers from the expedition - American Mallory Geis, Nadhira Ahmed Abdullah Al Harthy from Oman and Pur Bahadur Gurung from Nepal - had been recovered.

Purja's death was also confirmed by Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah, who said on social media that "the tragic death of six Nepalese and four other foreign climbers, including world record holder Nirmal Purja, in the Karakoram mountain range of Pakistan, has shocked us".

"The history of their courage, dedication, and contributions will always remain inspiring," the prime minister added.

Rescue teams in Pakistan had been searching for the climbers on the world's 12th-highest summit after an avalanche on the 8,047m (26,400ft) peak in the Karakoram range.

The multinational climbing group was being led by Purja. Also known as Nims, he rose to prominence in 2019 when he climbed all 14 of the world's mountains with peaks above 8,000m in 189 days - smashing the previous record by more than seven years.

The 43-year-old became widely known following a Netflix documentary chronicling his journey, 14 Peaks: Nothing Is Impossible, released two years later.

At the time, he said: "It has been a gruelling but humbling six months, and I hope to have proven that anything is possible with some determination, self-belief and positivity."

Purja served in the British military for 16 years, 10 of which were spent in the special forces, and he was awarded an MBE by the late Queen in 2018 for his achievement in extreme high-altitude mountaineering.

He said he was also the first Gurkha to climb Everest while serving in the British military.

In his last post on X, published on Monday, Purja said he had not intended to climb Broad Peak.

"Initially, the plan was to climb just G2," he wrote, referring to Gasherbrum II, another peak in the Karakoram mountain range.

But right before he set off for Pakistan, he realised that if he also managed to climb Broad Peak while he was there, he would have only one more mountain to conquer before becoming the "first person in history to climb all 14 eight-thousanders twice. Without oxygen."

An eight-thousander is a mountain that rises more than 8,000m above sea level.

"This wasn't planned," Purja wrote. "But opportunities don't scream: they whisper to those already working in silence."

"Broad Peak, I ask for nothing but safe passage up and back down. I take zero mountains for granted," he wrote.

Broad Peak is regarded as one of the more challenging mountains for climbers. The first successful ascent was in 1957, when an Austrian expedition reached the summit.

Since then, many more have climbed the mountain, but dozens have lost their lives.

One of Broad Peak's deadliest years was 2013, when at least six fatalities were recorded.
